text: Healthcare Services Chronic Disease Care In Woolloongabba Structured, ongoing general practice care for long-term health conditions, with monitoring, care planning and coordination over time. What is this service? Ongoing care for long-term health conditions. Chronic disease care supports people living with health conditions that need ongoing monitoring, treatment or coordination over time. Examples can include diabetes, heart and vascular conditions, asthma, COPD, arthritis and other complex or long-term health needs. General practice often acts as the central point for bringing together medicines, investigations, specialist advice, allied health input and the patient’s own goals. Why does it matter? Long-term conditions benefit from care that evolves over time. Symptoms, medicines, test results and personal circumstances can change. Regular review helps keep the care plan current, identify complications earlier and coordinate the different professionals involved in your care. Continuity is particularly valuable when you have more than one condition or take several medicines. How can we help? Monitoring, planning and coordination. Depending on your condition and individual needs, care may include: Regular clinical review and monitoring Medication review and treatment planning Chronic disease management planning where clinically appropriate Review of pathology, imaging and specialist correspondence Coordination with specialists and allied health practitioners Support for self-management, lifestyle goals and risk reduction Follow-up after hospital or specialist care Preventive healthcare relevant to your long-term condition Understanding your care Good chronic care is coordinated care. Keeping an accurate medication list and bringing recent specialist letters, discharge summaries or home monitoring information can help your GP see the whole picture. If several conditions or care plans need review, ask reception whether a longer appointment would be more suitable. This information is general in nature. Your practitioner can provide advice based on your individual health history and circumstances. What should I do next? Plan a review before problems become urgent. Book a review with your regular GP or a practitioner whose verified interests match your condition. Regular follow-up is usually more useful than waiting until a problem becomes urgent. Bring an up-to-date medication list, including non-prescription medicines if relevant. Bring recent specialist letters, results or home monitoring records you have been asked to keep. Ask whether a longer appointment is appropriate for complex or multiple conditions. Seek urgent medical care for sudden or severe symptoms; call 000 for a life-threatening emergency. text: Healthcare Services Family Healthcare In Woolloongabba Ongoing general practice care for individuals and families, with continuity across changing health needs and life stages. What is this service? Everyday healthcare with a long-term view. Family health is general practice care that supports people through everyday illness, preventive care, changing life stages and longer-term health needs. At Woolloongabba Medical Centre, family healthcare is centred on continuity. A regular practice can build an understanding of your history, medicines, previous investigations, family history and health priorities over time. Each person’s healthcare remains individual and confidential, even when several members of the same family attend the practice. Why does it matter? Continuity gives everyday healthcare more context. Health rarely fits into a single appointment. New symptoms may relate to previous conditions, medicines, family history or changes in work, family and lifestyle. Having a GP or practice that knows your history can improve continuity, reduce the need to start again at each visit and make it easier to coordinate preventive care, referrals and follow-up. How can we help? Care for everyday and ongoing health needs. Depending on your needs and clinical circumstances, family healthcare may include: General health concerns and acute illness Preventive healthcare and age-appropriate health discussions Medication review and ongoing prescriptions where clinically appropriate Management and monitoring of long-term conditions Children’s, women’s and men’s health Referrals to specialists or allied health when clinically appropriate Follow-up after investigations, hospital care or specialist review Understanding your care Making continuity work for you. Bring recent reports or specialist correspondence if they may help your GP understand what has changed. text: Healthcare Services Mental Health Care In Woolloongabba A confidential place to start the conversation, with GP assessment, ongoing support, treatment planning and referral where appropriate. What is this service? Primary healthcare for mental wellbeing. Mental health care in general practice can support people experiencing anxiety, low mood, stress, burnout, sleep concerns, adjustment difficulties or other changes in mental wellbeing. A GP can assess your symptoms, consider physical and mental health together, discuss treatment options and arrange referral to other mental health professionals where appropriate. When clinically appropriate, a GP may also prepare a Mental Health Treatment Plan to support structured treatment and eligible Medicare-rebated care. Why does it matter? Mental wellbeing is part of overall health. Mental health can affect sleep, relationships, work, study, physical symptoms and the ability to manage other health conditions. Early support can help clarify what is happening and what options are available. Seeing a practitioner you feel comfortable with can make it easier to discuss sensitive concerns and review progress over time. How can we help? Assessment, treatment planning and follow-up. Depending on your situation, GP mental health care may include: Assessment of symptoms and how they are affecting daily life Discussion of treatment and self-management options Mental Health Treatment Plans when clinically appropriate Medication discussion and review where appropriate Referral to psychologists, psychiatrists or other services when needed Follow-up to review progress, treatment response and changing needs Consideration of physical health issues that may affect mental wellbeing Understanding your care A mental health appointment can take time. It can help to book a longer appointment so there is enough time to discuss how you have been feeling, how long symptoms have been present and how they are affecting your daily life. You may wish to write down important symptoms, medicines and questions before the appointment. You can also ask about bringing a trusted support person if that would help you feel more comfortable. Ask reception whether a longer consultation is suitable. Choose a practitioner with a verified mental health interest if you prefer. Book enough time to discuss your concerns without feeling rushed. Bring your current medication list and any relevant mental health care information. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call Triple Zero (000). text: Healthcare Services Preventive Healthcare In Woolloongabba Planned health reviews, risk discussions and preventive care designed to support early action and long-term wellbeing. What is this service? Healthcare before a problem becomes urgent. Preventive healthcare focuses on reducing health risks, identifying concerns early and keeping recommended care up to date before symptoms become serious. In general practice, prevention may include age- and risk-appropriate screening discussions, immunisation review, lifestyle support, family-history assessment and monitoring of important health risks. Preventive care is not a fixed checklist. What is appropriate depends on your age, sex, medical history, family history, medicines and individual risk factors. Why does it matter? Prevention creates opportunities for earlier action. Some conditions develop gradually and may have few symptoms at first. Regular preventive care gives you and your GP an opportunity to review risk, discuss screening and identify changes that may benefit from follow-up. It also helps keep vaccinations, chronic disease risk and lifestyle goals connected to your broader health plan. How can we help? Risk review, screening and prevention. Preventive healthcare may include: General health and risk-factor review Age- and risk-appropriate screening discussions Blood pressure and other clinically appropriate health checks Vaccination and immunisation review Lifestyle, nutrition, physical activity and smoking discussions Family-history and cardiovascular risk review Women’s, men’s and children’s preventive health discussions Follow-up or referral when a risk or abnormal result needs further assessment Understanding your care Screening should be appropriate for you. More testing is not always better. Screening has benefits and limitations, and the right approach depends on your individual risk and current Australian recommendations. Your GP can explain why a particular check is or is not recommended and what should happen after a result. This information is general in nature. Your practitioner can provide advice based on your individual health history and circumstances. What should I do next? Book a preventive health discussion based on your own risks and history. If it has been some time since your last general health review, or if your family history or health risks have changed, book a preventive health discussion with a GP. Bring an up-to-date medication list and relevant family-health information. Tell your GP about changes in smoking, alcohol, exercise, weight or other health risks where relevant. Ask which vaccinations and screening programs are appropriate for you. Book follow-up if a result or risk factor needs further assessment. A longer appointment may help if several screening, lifestyle or risk-factor topics need review. Before your appointment Bring relevant screening history, vaccination records, family history and a current medicines list if available. After your appointment & follow-up Your GP will explain which screening or monitoring is appropriate, when it is due and how results will be followed up. text: Our Services Skin Checks in Woolloongabba Assessment of new, changing or concerning spots and lesions, with follow-up, minor procedures or referral when clinically appropriate. What is this service? A skin check is a clinical assessment of your skin and areas of concern. Skin checks can focus on a particular spot or involve a broader review depending on your reason for attending, history and risk factors. A GP can assess lesions and skin changes, discuss what they may represent and recommend an appropriate next step. If a lesion needs further assessment, the next step may include monitoring, a procedure such as biopsy or excision where appropriate, or referral for specialist care. Why does it matter? Changes in the skin are worth assessing early. Many skin spots and lesions are not cancer, but new, changing or unusual areas should not be ignored. Clinical assessment can help distinguish changes that can be monitored from those that need further investigation or treatment. Your individual risk can be influenced by factors such as previous skin cancer, sun exposure, skin type, family history and the appearance or behaviour of a lesion. How can we help? Assessment, monitoring and next-step planning. Depending on your needs and clinical assessment, care may include: Assessment of new or changing spots and lesions Review of areas that itch, bleed, crust, change shape or otherwise concern you Discussion of personal and family skin-cancer history Clinical examination and risk-based follow-up planning Minor procedures such as biopsy or excision when clinically appropriate and available Referral for specialist assessment when required Preventive advice, including sun-protection discussions Ongoing review where your practitioner recommends follow-up Understanding your care Know your skin and seek assessment when something changes. Between appointments, being familiar with your own skin can help you notice a spot or lesion that is new or changing. A photograph may help document a change over time, but it does not replace clinical assessment. There is no single skin-check interval that is right for everyone. Your practitioner can recommend follow-up based on your individual history, examination and risk factors. This information is general in nature. Your practitioner can provide advice based on your individual health history and circumstances. What should I do next? Book a skin-check appointment for new, changing or concerning areas. Tell reception if you want a focused lesion review or a broader skin-check appointment so appropriate time can be considered. Bring information about previous skin cancers, biopsies or relevant specialist reports if available. Avoid delaying assessment of a lesion that is changing rapidly, bleeding repeatedly or otherwise causing concern. Call 000 for a life-threatening emergency; skin concerns that are urgent but not life-threatening should be assessed promptly through an appropriate clinical service. Planning your appointment Booking, preparation, follow-up and costs. How to book Book a skin-check appointment or ask reception which appointment type is appropriate. Mention a rapidly changing or concerning lesion when booking. Before your appointment If possible, avoid heavy makeup, nail polish over a concerning nail lesion, or clothing that makes the area difficult to examine. Bring previous skin-cancer history if not already known to the practice. After your appointment & follow-up Your clinician will explain whether routine observation, photography, biopsy, excision or referral is recommended and when the next review should occur. Procedures, consumables, medicines or devices, reports and other non-Medicare services may attract additional fees. More information Cancer Council Australia — Check for signs of skin cancer Patient questions Frequently Asked Questions What happens during a skin check? Your practitioner will ask about the reason for the visit and relevant history, examine the area or areas of concern and discuss whether monitoring, a procedure, referral or another next step is appropriate. Do I need a referral for a GP skin check? No referral is generally required to book a GP appointment at the practice. If specialist assessment is needed after your review, your GP can discuss referral options. Can a GP biopsy or remove a skin lesion? Some practitioners provide selected minor skin procedures when clinically appropriate. text: Our Services Skin Cancer Care in Woolloongabba Assessment and coordinated next-step care for suspicious skin lesions, with procedures, pathology follow-up or specialist referral when clinically appropriate. What is this service? Skin cancer care begins with careful assessment and a clear next-step plan. Skin cancer care in general practice can include assessment of suspicious lesions, discussion of risk and appropriate follow-up when a spot needs more than routine observation. Depending on the clinical findings and the practitioner providing your care, the next step may include monitoring, a minor procedure such as biopsy or excision, pathology review or referral for specialist assessment. Why does it matter? Early assessment helps patients act on concerning skin changes. Many skin lesions are benign, but some need prompt investigation. A new or changing lesion, or one that bleeds, crusts, changes colour or shape, or otherwise concerns you, should be assessed rather than ignored. Your individual risk can also be influenced by previous skin cancer, sun exposure, skin type, family history and previous pathology. How can we help? Assessment, procedures, pathology follow-up and referral where appropriate. Care may include: Clinical assessment of suspicious or changing lesions Review of personal and family skin-cancer history Discussion of monitoring and follow-up intervals Selected minor procedures, including biopsy or excision, where clinically appropriate and available Review and explanation of pathology results Planning further treatment when a diagnosis requires it Referral for specialist assessment or treatment when needed Preventive advice about sun exposure and monitoring your skin Understanding your care A diagnosis may involve more than one step. Assessment does not always provide a final diagnosis immediately. If tissue is sent to pathology, your practitioner will explain how results will be followed up and what happens next. If you have previous pathology, specialist letters or photographs showing how a lesion has changed, bring them to your appointment when available. This information is general in nature. Your practitioner can provide advice based on your individual history and examination. What should I do next? Book an assessment if you have a lesion that concerns you. When booking, tell reception if the appointment is for a particular lesion, a broader skin review, or follow-up after a previous biopsy or procedure. text: Medical Procedures Iron Infusions Intravenous iron can replenish iron stores when a clinician has confirmed iron deficiency and an infusion is appropriate for your circumstances. Procedure information What this care involves. An iron infusion delivers iron directly into a vein. It may be considered when oral iron is not suitable, has not worked well enough, is not absorbed adequately, or when iron needs to be replaced more quickly. A clinician must first review the reason for low iron and confirm that an infusion is appropriate. What happens during the appointment? A nurse or doctor inserts an intravenous line, and the prescribed iron is given through a drip. You will be observed during the infusion and for the period the clinical team considers appropriate afterwards. Tell the team immediately if you feel unwell, develop pain around the IV site, or notice symptoms of a reaction. This page provides general information only. The treating clinician will explain what is appropriate for your individual circumstances and obtain consent where a procedure is planned. Before your appointment How to book and prepare. A GP review and recent blood results are usually needed first so the clinician can confirm the indication, the medicine and dose, and whether the infusion can be safely provided at the practice. Depending on the treatment plan, you may be asked to obtain the prescribed iron medicine from a pharmacy before the infusion; the practice will confirm this with you. After your appointment Follow-up and aftercare. Most people can resume normal activities after a routine infusion unless the treating clinician advises otherwise. Follow-up blood tests and/or a review appointment may be arranged to confirm that iron stores and haemoglobin have responded and to address the underlying cause of iron deficiency. text: Medical Procedures IUD Insertion & Removal An intrauterine device (IUD) is a long-acting reversible contraceptive placed inside the uterus by a trained clinician. Choosing an IUD involves a discussion about your health history, contraception goals, expected bleeding changes, benefits, risks and alternatives. Insertion and removal require trained-practitioner availability. What happens during the appointment? During insertion, the clinician places the IUD through the cervix into the uterus. At the appointment, your clinician will confirm whether you are due, discuss your screening history and explain your options. text: Medical Procedures Prostate Care Prostate care includes assessment of urinary symptoms, prostate-related concerns, risk factors and informed discussion about PSA testing when appropriate. Procedure information What this care involves. Prostate symptoms can have several causes, including benign enlargement, infection or other conditions. PSA testing can provide useful information in some situations but does not diagnose prostate cancer by itself. Decisions about testing are best made after discussing symptoms, age, family history and personal preferences. What happens during the appointment? Your doctor will take a history, review urinary or other symptoms and may perform a physical examination. Book Appointment Call (07) 3217 3344 Before your appointment Bring previous PSA results, urology reports, a current medicines list and information about family history if available. If a PSA test is planned, your clinician or pathology provider may give preparation instructions because some activities or conditions can temporarily affect PSA levels. After your appointment Follow-up and aftercare. Your doctor will review results in context. A raised PSA does not by itself mean cancer, and further assessment may include repeat testing, imaging or specialist referral. Follow the review plan provided by your clinician. Changes in urinary flow, frequency, urgency, difficulty passing urine, blood in urine or semen, or other new symptoms should be assessed. What happens if my PSA is elevated? Your doctor will consider possible causes and may recommend repeat testing, imaging or specialist assessment depending on the result and your risk profile. text: Medical Procedures Ear Care & Ear Syringing Ear care may include examination of the ear canal, treatment advice for wax build-up, and ear irrigation (often called ear syringing) when it is clinically appropriate. Procedure information What this care involves. Blocked ears, reduced hearing, discomfort or a feeling of fullness can sometimes be caused by ear wax, but other ear conditions can cause similar symptoms. The ear should be assessed before irrigation because syringing is not appropriate when there is certain ear disease, injury or infection. What happens during the appointment? A clinician examines the ear first. If wax is the likely cause and irrigation is suitable, body-temperature water may be used to gently flush wax from the ear canal. If the wax cannot be safely removed, another approach or referral may be recommended. This page provides general information only. The treating clinician will explain what is appropriate for your individual circumstances and obtain consent where a procedure is planned. Before your appointment How to book and prepare. How to book Call reception if you are specifically seeking ear syringing so the correct appointment type can be arranged. A GP or nurse assessment may be needed before the procedure. Book Appointment Call (07) 3217 3344 Before your appointment Wax-softening drops may be recommended before irrigation, but they are not appropriate for everyone. Follow the instructions given by the practice rather than starting drops if you have a history of eardrum perforation, ear surgery, infection or other significant ear problems. After your appointment Follow-up and aftercare. Mild temporary discomfort can occur. Contact the practice if you develop persistent pain, discharge, dizziness, worsening hearing or other concerning symptoms. If wax cannot be removed safely, a referral may be recommended. Costs Know about fees before you attend. Exact additional fees are confirmed before treatment. The standard Medicare-eligible GP consultation is bulk billed in line with the practice billing policy. Ear syringing or related treatment may involve an additional procedure and consumable fee. Reception will confirm the current practice charge before the procedure is booked wherever practical. Any external specialist service is billed separately by that provider. Read Fees & Billing Patient questions Frequently Asked Questions Do all blocked ears need syringing? No. Ear blockage has different causes, and irrigation is not suitable for every ear. The ear should be assessed first. Should I use wax-softening drops before my appointment? Only if the practice or your clinician recommends them for you. Tell the team about previous eardrum perforation, ear surgery or infection. Can cotton buds remove ear wax? Objects placed into the ear canal can push wax deeper or injure the ear. Healthdirect advises against trying to pick wax out with cotton buds or other objects. What if the wax cannot be removed? The clinician may recommend another treatment method or referral to an ear, nose and throat service. More information Trusted information and related care. text: Medical Procedures Spirometry Spirometry is a lung-function test that measures how much air you can breathe out and how quickly you can breathe it out. Procedure information What this care involves. Spirometry can help assess breathing symptoms and support diagnosis or monitoring of conditions such as asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Results are interpreted alongside your history, examination and other tests. What happens during the appointment? You will be asked to take a full breath and blow hard and fast into a mouthpiece connected to a spirometer. The test is repeated to obtain reliable measurements. In some situations, testing may be repeated after an inhaled medicine. This page provides general information only. The treating clinician will explain what is appropriate for your individual circumstances and obtain consent where a procedure is planned. Before your appointment How to book and prepare. How to book Call reception if you have been asked to have spirometry so the practice can confirm availability, appointment length and whether you need a GP assessment before or after the test. Book Appointment Call (07) 3217 3344 Before your appointment Preparation can vary. You may receive instructions about smoking, food, exercise or inhaler use before the test. Do not stop prescribed inhalers or other medicines unless the practice specifically tells you to do so. After your appointment Follow-up and aftercare. Your clinician will review the measurements in the context of your symptoms and medical history. Should I stop my inhaler before the test? Only if the practice specifically instructs you to do so. Preparation depends on why the test is being performed. Is spirometry painful? No, but the repeated forced breathing can be tiring or make some people briefly light-headed. Tell the clinician if you feel unwell. Will spirometry give me a diagnosis by itself? Not usually. Results are interpreted together with your symptoms, medical history and other clinical information. More information Trusted information and related care. text: Medical Procedures Nebulising A nebuliser converts liquid medicine into a fine mist that can be breathed into the lungs through a mask or mouthpiece. For many people with asthma, a puffer with a spacer can be as effective as a nebuliser. Severe breathing difficulty is an emergency and should not wait for a routine appointment. What happens during the appointment? If nebulised treatment is indicated, the medicine is placed in the nebuliser and inhaled through a mask or mouthpiece while you are monitored.
